11056!> \namespace mom_hor_visc
11057!!
11058!! \section section_horizontal_viscosity Horizontal viscosity in MOM
11059!!
11060!! This module contains the subroutine horizontal_viscosity that calculates the
11061!! effects of horizontal viscosity, including parameterizations of the value of
11062!! the viscosity itself. Subroutine horizontal_viscosity calculates the acceleration due to
11063!! some combination of a biharmonic viscosity and a Laplacian viscosity. Either or
11064!! both may use a coefficient that depends on the shear and strain of the flow.
11065!! All metric terms are retained. The Laplacian is calculated as the divergence of
11066!! a stress tensor, using the form suggested by \cite Smagorinsky1993. The biharmonic
11067!! is calculated by twice applying the divergence of the stress tensor that is
11068!! used to calculate the Laplacian, but without the dependence on thickness in the
11069!! first pass. This form permits a variable viscosity, and indicates no
11070!! acceleration for either resting fluid or solid body rotation.
11071!!
11072!! The form of the viscous accelerations is discussed extensively in \cite griffies2000,
11073!! and the implementation here follows that discussion closely.
11074!! We use the notation of \cite Smith2003 with the exception that the
11075!! isotropic viscosity is \f$\kappa_h\f$.
11076!!
11077!! In general, the horizontal stress tensor can be written as
11078!! \f[
11079!! {\bf \sigma} =
11080!! \begin{pmatrix}
11081!! \frac{1}{2} \left( \sigma_D + \sigma_T \right) & \frac{1}{2} \sigma_S \\\\
11082!! \frac{1}{2} \sigma_S & \frac{1}{2} \left( \sigma_D - \sigma_T \right)
11083!! \end{pmatrix}
11084!! \f]
11085!! where \f$\sigma_D\f$, \f$\sigma_T\f$ and \f$\sigma_S\f$ are stresses associated with
11086!! invariant factors in the strain-rate tensor. For a Newtonian fluid, the stress
11087!! tensor is usually linearly related to the strain-rate tensor. The horizontal
11088!! strain-rate tensor is
11089!! \f[
11090!! \dot{\bf e} =
11091!! \begin{pmatrix}
11092!! \frac{1}{2} \left( \dot{e}_D + \dot{e}_T \right) & \frac{1}{2} \dot{e}_S \\\\
11093!! \frac{1}{2} \dot{e}_S & \frac{1}{2} \left( \dot{e}_D - \dot{e}_T \right)
11094!! \end{pmatrix}
11095!! \f]
11096!! where \f$\dot{e}_D = \partial_x u + \partial_y v\f$ is the horizontal divergence,
11097!! \f$\dot{e}_T = \partial_x u - \partial_y v\f$ is the horizontal tension, and
11098!! \f$\dot{e}_S = \partial_y u + \partial_x v\f$ is the horizontal shear strain.
11099!!
11100!! The trace of the stress tensor, \f$tr(\bf \sigma) = \sigma_D\f$, is usually
11101!! absorbed into the pressure and only the deviatoric stress tensor considered.
11102!! From here on, we drop \f$\sigma_D\f$. The trace of the strain tensor, \f$tr(\bf e) =
11103!! \dot{e}_D\f$ is non-zero for horizontally divergent flow but only enters the
11104!! stress tensor through \f$\sigma_D\f$ and so we will drop \f$\sigma_D\f$ from
11105!! calculations of the strain tensor in the code. Therefore the horizontal stress
11106!! tensor can be considered to be
11107!! \f[
11108!! {\bf \sigma} =
11109!! \begin{pmatrix}
11110!! \frac{1}{2} \sigma_T & \frac{1}{2} \sigma_S \\\\
11111!! \frac{1}{2} \sigma_S & - \frac{1}{2} \sigma_T
11112!! \end{pmatrix}
11113!! .\f]
11114!!
11115!! The stresses above are linearly related to the strain through a viscosity
11116!! coefficient, \f$\kappa_h\f$:
11117!! \f{eqnarray*}{
11118!! \sigma_T & = & 2 \kappa_h \dot{e}_T \\\\
11119!! \sigma_S & = & 2 \kappa_h \dot{e}_S
11120!! .
11121!! \f}
11122!!
11123!! The viscosity \f$\kappa_h\f$ may either be a constant or variable. For example,
11124!! \f$\kappa_h\f$ may vary with the shear, as proposed by \cite Smagorinsky1993.
11125!!
11126!! The accelerations resulting form the divergence of the stress tensor are
11127!! \f{eqnarray*}{
11128!! \hat{\bf x} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot {\bf \sigma} \right)
11129!! & = &
11130!! \partial_x \left( \frac{1}{2} \sigma_T \right)
11131!! + \partial_y \left( \frac{1}{2} \sigma_S \right)
11132!! \\\\
11133!! & = &
11134!! \partial_x \left( \kappa_h \dot{e}_T \right)
11135!! + \partial_y \left( \kappa_h \dot{e}_S \right)
11136!! \\\\
11137!! \hat{\bf y} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot {\bf \sigma} \right)
11138!! & = &
11139!! \partial_x \left( \frac{1}{2} \sigma_S \right)
11140!! + \partial_y \left( - \frac{1}{2} \sigma_T \right)
11141!! \\\\
11142!! & = &
11143!! \partial_x \left( \kappa_h \dot{e}_S \right)
11144!! + \partial_y \left( - \kappa_h \dot{e}_T \right)
11145!! .
11146!! \f}
11147!!
11148!! The form of the Laplacian viscosity in general coordinates is:
11149!! \f{eqnarray*}{
11150!! \hat{\bf x} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot \sigma \right)
11151!! & = &
11152!! \frac{1}{h} \left[ \partial_x \left( \kappa_h h \dot{e}_T \right)
11153!! + \partial_y \left( \kappa_h h \dot{e}_S \right) \right]
11154!! \\\\
11155!! \hat{\bf y} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot \sigma \right)
11156!! & = &
11157!! \frac{1}{h} \left[ \partial_x \left( \kappa_h h \dot{e}_S \right)
11158!! - \partial_y \left( \kappa_h h \dot{e}_T \right) \right]
11159!! .
11160!! \f}
11161!!
11162!! \subsection section_laplacian_viscosity_coefficient Laplacian viscosity coefficient
11163!!
11164!! The horizontal viscosity coefficient, \f$\kappa_h\f$, can have multiple components.
11165!! The isotropic components are:
11166!! - A uniform background component, \f$\kappa_{bg}\f$.
11167!! - A constant but spatially variable 2D map, \f$\kappa_{2d}(x,y)\f$.
11168!! - A ''MICOM'' viscosity, \f$U_\nu \Delta(x,y)\f$, which uses a constant
11169!! velocity scale, \f$U_\nu\f$ and a measure of the grid-spacing \f$\Delta(x,y)^2 =
11170!! \frac{2 \Delta x^2 \Delta y^2}{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}\f$.
11171!! - A function of
11172!! latitude, \f$\kappa_{\phi}(x,y) = \kappa_{\pi/2} |\sin(\phi)|^n\f$.
11173!! - A dynamic Smagorinsky viscosity, \f$\kappa_{Sm}(x,y,t) = C_{Sm} \Delta^2 \sqrt{\dot{e}_T^2 + \dot{e}_S^2}\f$.
11174!! - A dynamic Leith viscosity, \f$\kappa_{Lth}(x,y,t) =
11175!! C_{Lth} \Delta^3 \sqrt{|\nabla \zeta|^2 + |\nabla \dot{e}_D|^2}\f$.
11176!!
11177!! A maximum stable viscosity, \f$\kappa_{max}(x,y)\f$ is calculated based on the
11178!! grid-spacing and time-step and used to clip calculated viscosities.
11179!!
11180!! The static components of \f$\kappa_h\f$ are first combined as follows:
11181!! \f[
11182!! \kappa_{static} = \min \left[ \max\left(
11183!! \kappa_{bg},
11184!! U_\nu \Delta(x,y),
11185!! \kappa_{2d}(x,y),
11186!! \kappa_\phi(x,y)
11187!! \right)
11188!! , \kappa_{max}(x,y) \right]
11189!! \f]
11190!! and stored in the module control structure as variables <code>Kh_bg_xx</code> and
11191!! <code>Kh_bg_xy</code> for the tension (h-points) and shear (q-points) components
11192!! respectively.
11193!!
11194!! The full viscosity includes the dynamic components as follows:
11195!! \f[
11196!! \kappa_h(x,y,t) = r(\Delta,L_d)
11197!! \max \left( \kappa_{static}, \kappa_{Sm}, \kappa_{Lth} \right)
11198!! \f]
11199!! where \f$r(\Delta,L_d)\f$ is a resolution function.
11200!!
11201!! The dynamic Smagorinsky and Leith viscosity schemes are exclusive with each
11202!! other.
11203!!
11204!! \subsection section_viscous_boundary_conditions Viscous boundary conditions
11205!!
11206!! Free slip boundary conditions have been coded, although no slip boundary
11207!! conditions can be used with the Laplacian viscosity based on the 2D land-sea
11208!! mask. For a western boundary, for example, the boundary conditions with the
11209!! biharmonic operator would be written as:
11210!! \f[
11211!! \partial_x v = 0 ; \partial_x^3 v = 0 ; u = 0 ; \partial_x^2 u = 0 ,
11212!! \f]
11213!! while for a Laplacian operator, they are simply
11214!! \f[
11215!! \partial_x v = 0 ; u = 0 .
11216!! \f]
11217!! These boundary conditions are largely dictated by the use of an Arakawa
11218!! C-grid and by the varying layer thickness.
11219!!
11220!! \subsection section_anisotropic_viscosity Anisotropic viscosity
11221!!
11222!! \cite Large2001 proposed enhancing viscosity in a particular direction and the
11223!! approach was generalized in \cite Smith2003. We use the second form of their
11224!! two coefficient anisotropic viscosity (section 4.3). We also replace their
11225!! \f$A^\prime\f$ and $D$ such that \f$2A^\prime = 2 \kappa_h + D\f$ and
11226!! \f$\kappa_a = D\f$ so that \f$\kappa_h\f$ can be considered the isotropic
11227!! viscosity and \f$\kappa_a=D\f$ can be consider the anisotropic viscosity. The
11228!! direction of anisotropy is defined by a unit vector \f$\hat{\bf
11229!! n}=(n_1,n_2)\f$.
11230!!
11231!! The contributions to the stress tensor are
11232!! \f[
11233!! \begin{pmatrix}
11234!! \sigma_T \\\\ \sigma_S
11235!! \end{pmatrix}
11236!! =
11237!! \left[
11238!! \begin{pmatrix}
11239!! 2 \kappa_h + \kappa_a & 0 \\\\
11240!! 0 & 2 \kappa_h
11241!! \end{pmatrix}
11242!! + 2 \kappa_a n_1 n_2
11243!! \begin{pmatrix}
11244!! - 2 n_1 n_2 & n_1^2 - n_2^2 \\\\
11245!! n_1^2 - n_2^2 & 2 n_1 n_2
11246!! \end{pmatrix}
11247!! \right]
11248!! \begin{pmatrix}
11249!! \dot{e}_T \\\\ \dot{e}_S
11250!! \end{pmatrix}
11251!! \f]
11252!! Dissipation of kinetic energy requires \f$\kappa_h \geq 0\f$ and \f$2 \kappa_h + \kappa_a \geq 0\f$.
11253!! Note that when anisotropy is aligned with the x-direction, \f$n_1 = \pm 1\f$, then
11254!! \f$n_2 = 0\f$ and the cross terms vanish. The accelerations in this aligned limit
11255!! with constant coefficients become
11256!! \f{eqnarray*}{
11257!! \hat{\bf x} \cdot \nabla \cdot {\bf \sigma}
11258!! & = &
11259!! \partial_x \left( \left( \kappa_h + \frac{1}{2} \kappa_a \right) \dot{e}_T \right)
11260!! + \partial_y \left( \kappa_h \dot{e}_S \right)
11261!! \\\\
11262!! & = &
11263!! \left( \kappa_h + \kappa_a \right) \partial_{xx} u
11264!! + \kappa_h \partial_{yy} u
11265!! - \frac{1}{2} \kappa_a \partial_x \left( \partial_x u + \partial_y v \right)
11266!! \\\\
11267!! \hat{\bf y} \cdot \nabla \cdot {\bf \sigma}
11268!! & = &
11269!! \partial_x \left( \kappa_h \dot{e}_S \right)
11270!! - \partial_y \left( \left( \kappa_h + \frac{1}{2} \kappa_a \right) \dot{e}_T \right)
11271!! \\\\
11272!! & = &
11273!! \kappa_h \partial_{xx} v
11274!! + \left( \kappa_h + \kappa_a \right) \partial_{yy} v
11275!! - \frac{1}{2} \kappa_a \partial_y \left( \partial_x u + \partial_y v \right)
11276!! \f}
11277!! which has contributions akin to a negative divergence damping (a divergence
11278!! enhancement?) but which is weaker than the enhanced tension terms by half.
11279!!
11280!! \subsection section_viscous_discretization Discretization
11281!!
11282!! The horizontal tension, \f$\dot{e}_T\f$, is stored in variable <code>sh_xx</code> and
11283!! discretized as
11284!! \f[
11285!! \dot{e}_T
11286!! = \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} \delta_i \left( \frac{1}{\Delta y} u \right)
11287!! - \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} \delta_j \left( \frac{1}{\Delta x} v \right)
11288!! .
11289!! \f]
11290!! The horizontal divergent strain, \f$\dot{e}_D\f$, is stored in variable
11291!! <code>div_xx</code> and discretized as
11292!! \f[
11293!! \dot{e}_D
11294!! = \frac{1}{h A} \left( \delta_i \left( \overline{h}^i \Delta y \, u \right)
11295!! + \delta_j \left( \overline{h}^j\Delta x \, v \right) \right)
11296!! .
11297!! \f]
11298!! Note that for expediency this is the exact discretization used in the
11299!! continuity equation.
11300!!
11301!! The horizontal shear strain, \f$\dot{e}_S\f$, is stored in variable <code>sh_xy</code>
11302!! and discretized as
11303!! \f[
11304!! \dot{e}_S = v_x + u_y
11305!! \f]
11306!! where
11307!! \f{align*}{
11308!! v_x &= \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} \delta_i \left( \frac{1}{\Delta y} v \right) \\\\
11309!! u_y &= \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} \delta_j \left( \frac{1}{\Delta x} u \right)
11310!! \f}
11311!! which are calculated separately so that no-slip or free-slip boundary
11312!! conditions can be applied to \f$v_x\f$ and \f$u_y\f$ where appropriate.
11313!!
11314!! The tendency for the x-component of the divergence of stress is stored in
11315!! variable <code>diffu</code> and discretized as
11316!! \f[
11317!! \hat{\bf x} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot {\bf \sigma} \right) =
11318!! \frac{1}{A \overline{h}^i} \left(
11319!! \frac{1}{\Delta y} \delta_i \left( h \Delta y^2 \kappa_h \dot{e}_T \right) +
11320!! \frac{1}{\Delta x} \delta_j \left( \tilde{h}^{ij} \Delta x^2 \kappa_h \dot{e}_S \right)
11321!! \right)
11322!! .
11323!! \f]
11324!!
11325!! The tendency for the y-component of the divergence of stress is stored in
11326!! variable <code>diffv</code> and discretized as
11327!! \f[
11328!! \hat{\bf y} \cdot \left( \nabla \cdot {\bf \sigma} \right) =
11329!! \frac{1}{A \overline{h}^j} \left(
11330!! \frac{1}{\Delta y} \delta_i \left( \tilde{h}^{ij} \Delta y^2 A_M \dot{e}_S \right)
11331!! - \frac{1}{\Delta x} \delta_j \left( h \Delta x^2 A_M \dot{e}_T \right)
11332!! \right)
11333!! .
11334!! \f]
11335!!

11337!!

11339!! Smagorinsky-like viscosity for use in large-scale eddy-permitting ocean models.
11340!! Monthly Weather Review, 128(8), 2935-2946.
11341!! https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0493(2000)128%3C2935:BFWASL%3E2.0.CO;2
11342!!
11343!! Large, W.G., Danabasoglu, G., McWilliams, J.C., Gent, P.R. and Bryan, F.O.,
11344!! 2001: Equatorial circulation of a global ocean climate model with
11345!! anisotropic horizontal viscosity.
11346!! Journal of Physical Oceanography, 31(2), pp.518-536.
11347!! https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0485(2001)031%3C0518:ECOAGO%3E2.0.CO;2
11348!!
11349!! Smagorinsky, J., 1993: Some historical remarks on the use of nonlinear
11350!! viscosities. Large eddy simulation of complex engineering and geophysical
11351!! flows, 1, 69-106.
11352!!
11353!! Smith, R.D., and McWilliams, J.C., 2003: Anisotropic horizontal viscosity for
11354!! ocean models. Ocean Modelling, 5(2), 129-156.
11355!! https://doi.org/10.1016/S1463-5003(02)00016-1
113560end module MOM_hor_visc
